# M05 — Regime-aware models (Phase 5)

*Generated by `python -m src.experiments.run_regime_lstm` on 2026-08-24 02:36 UTC. Numbers trace to `results/tables/m05_regime_dl_*` and `results/predictions/m05_regime_dl_*.parquet`.*

## Scope

Roadmap Phase 5 (Ch2 §2.5): condition the Phase-3 **LSTM** on the Phase-4 regime signal from the **jump-penalised HMM** (Nystrup, Lindström & Madsen 2020 — the estimator Ch2 §2.4/§2.8 adopts) and test whether it improves daily realized-variance forecasts on the same leakage-free anchored walk-forward as Phases 2–3 (**RQ2**). The signal is the **causal filtered** posterior P(sₜ|x₁..xₜ) from Phase 4 (`jphmm_filt_p0`, `jphmm_filt_p1`, `jphmm_filt_p2`); it is lagged one day so a forecast for RVₜ only ever conditions on the regime known at t−1. Hyperparameters are fixed at the Phase-3 selection (hidden 128, lookback 10, lr 1e-3), so 'LSTM → Regime-LSTM' isolates regime-conditioning rather than a new sweep.

> **Refit cadence (read with every number below).** As in Phase 3, the deep models use `refit_every_folds: 0`: each network is trained **once** on all pre-test data (≤ 2018-12-31) and then frozen across the whole 2019 → Feb-2022 out-of-sample window, while GARCH/EGARCH/HAR-RV are refit every 21 trading days on an expanding window. Both schemes are leakage-free, but they are not symmetric: by February 2022 the econometric baselines have seen three more years of data than the networks, including the COVID crash. The asymmetry therefore runs **against** the deep models, so their wins are conservative — and any deep-model weakness in the high-volatility states cannot be separated from the staleness of their training window on this evidence alone. Chapter 3 states this; a `refit_every_folds: 1` sensitivity is Phase-8 work.

Two architectures (roadmap Phase 5):
- **Regime-LSTM-A** — regime as feature: filtered posteriors appended to the LSTM input (Ch2 §2.5). `Regime-LSTM-A-RVonly` is the same on HAR-RV's exact input set (RV history only), matched to the Phase-3 winner.
- **Regime-LSTM-B** — regime-specific experts: one LSTM per regime, soft-gated by the posterior at t−1 (mixture-of-experts).

## Per-regime breakdown (RQ2)

QLIKE within each regime over the test window. **A day is bucketed by the regime known at t−1**, not by the regime the filter assigns to that day. This is a methodological choice and it changes the answer: the causal filtered state sₜ is inferred *using the day-t return*, so bucketing day t's error by sₜ would sort days by the very outcome whose error is being measured inside the bucket. Only the t−1 label makes "the edge is concentrated in state k" a claim about something a user of the model actually knew, and it is the same label the regime-aware models condition on and the same one the Giacomini–White test below is given.

| all | 784 | 0.2745 | 0.2650 | 0.2596 | 0.2632 | 0.2617 | 0.2621 |

The two tables differ on **52 of 784 days (6.6%)** — the regime-*transition* days, whose bucket is decided by the labelling convention alone. That is the entire gap between them, and it is why a per-regime ranking that flips between conventions is evidence about the convention, not about the models.

## Significance — formal DM + Model Confidence Set

Pairwise **Diebold–Mariano** (1995) on the QLIKE differential, with the Harvey–Leybourne–Newbold (1997) small-sample correction and a Student-t reference (a negative statistic means the first model has the lower loss). The **Model Confidence Set** (Hansen, Lunde & Nason 2011) then controls for multiple comparison across *all* models jointly (Ch2 §2.7).

| comparison (a vs b) | DM stat | p | better | n |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Regime-LSTM-A vs LSTM | -0.44 | 0.658 | Regime-LSTM-A | 784 |
| Regime-LSTM-A vs HAR-RV | -0.74 | 0.462 | Regime-LSTM-A | 784 |
| Regime-LSTM-B vs LSTM | -0.61 | 0.544 | Regime-LSTM-B | 784 |
| Regime-LSTM-B vs HAR-RV | -0.74 | 0.459 | Regime-LSTM-B | 784 |
| Regime-LSTM-A-RVonly vs LSTM-RVonly | 0.48 | 0.629 | LSTM-RVonly | 784 |
| Regime-LSTM-A-RVonly vs HAR-RV | -1.32 | 0.188 | Regime-LSTM-A-RVonly | 784 |

**Model Confidence Set — 90% confidence.** QLIKE loss; stationary bootstrap (2000 reps, block 10, 'R' statistic, seed 17). Surviving set = {HAR-RV, LSTM, LSTM-RVonly, Regime-LSTM-A, Regime-LSTM-A-RVonly, Regime-LSTM-B}; eliminated = {EGARCH, GARCH, RW-RV}.

## Findings (RQ2)

The overall best model on the board is **LSTM-RVonly** (QLIKE **0.2596**), ahead of the regime-agnostic LSTM 0.2650 and HAR-RV 0.2745.

**Regime conditioning does not have a consistent pooled sign.** Compared only against its own regime-agnostic twin — the same features, the same hyperparameters, the regime posterior added — it helps in 2 of 3 matched pairs and hurts in 1: Regime-LSTM-A 0.2632 vs LSTM 0.2650 (−0.0018); Regime-LSTM-A-RVonly 0.2617 vs LSTM-RVonly 0.2596 (+0.0021); Regime-LSTM-B 0.2621 vs LSTM 0.2650 (−0.0029). None of these gaps is significant (see the DM table above); note in particular that the best pooled model on the board carries **no** regime signal.

No pooled pairwise gap reaches significance on 784 days. Against the tougher, lower-parameter HAR-RV benchmark the gap is not significant (DM -1.32, p=0.188) — consistent with the Phase-3 result and the literature that HAR-RV is hard to beat on its native target. The 90% **Model Confidence Set** retains {HAR-RV, LSTM, LSTM-RVonly, Regime-LSTM-A, Regime-LSTM-A-RVonly, Regime-LSTM-B} and rejects {EGARCH, GARCH, RW-RV}: the deep-learning/HAR cluster is statistically inseparable on 784 days, while the GARCH family and the random-walk floor are excluded outright.

**A majority of matched pairs favours regime conditioning in every state** — on margins this small, read that as 'no clear harm', not as a win. **calm** (n=379): 2/3 matched pairs favour the regime model — Regime-LSTM-A 0.3164 vs LSTM 0.3187 (-0.7%), Regime-LSTM-A-RVonly 0.2920 vs LSTM-RVonly 0.2829 (+3.2%), Regime-LSTM-B 0.3172 vs LSTM 0.3187 (-0.5%); **transitional** (n=329): 2/3 matched pairs favour the regime model — Regime-LSTM-A 0.1945 vs LSTM 0.1921 (+1.3%), Regime-LSTM-A-RVonly 0.2158 vs LSTM-RVonly 0.2182 (-1.1%), Regime-LSTM-B 0.1851 vs LSTM 0.1921 (-3.6%); **crisis** (n=76): 2/3 matched pairs favour the regime model — Regime-LSTM-A 0.2952 vs LSTM 0.3131 (-5.7%), Regime-LSTM-A-RVonly 0.3099 vs LSTM-RVonly 0.3232 (-4.1%), Regime-LSTM-B 0.3211 vs LSTM 0.3131 (+2.6%).

Every one of those matched gaps lies between 0.5% and 5.7% of the baseline's QLIKE, on buckets of 76–379 days, with **no significance test attached** — the direction of a majority vote across three pairs is not evidence of an effect at these magnitudes. The Giacomini–White test referenced below is what settles it, and it localises the only surviving effect in the transitional state.

For reference, the best-of-each-family comparison — lowest of 3 regime models against lowest of 3 baselines within each bucket — reads: calm Regime-LSTM-A-RVonly 0.2920 vs LSTM-RVonly 0.2829 (3.2% higher); transitional Regime-LSTM-B 0.1851 vs LSTM 0.1921 (3.6% lower); crisis Regime-LSTM-A 0.2952 vs HAR-RV 0.3070 (3.8% lower). **Treat that line as descriptive only.** Taking a minimum over several models inside a bucket is a selection statistic with no error bar attached; it will show a margin in favour of whichever family has more entries even when every individual contrast is noise, and which architecture supplies the minimum changes from state to state.

Two cautions belong with this table rather than after it. First, the split is still *descriptive*: it reports point estimates per bucket, and the pooled DM tests above are the only significance evidence attached to it — run `python -m src.experiments.report_gw` for the Giacomini–White conditional test and the per-regime DM columns, which use the same t−1 indicators and are the properly sized way to ask whether the loss difference is regime-dependent. On the current board only the **transitional** state survives that test; the calm and crisis contrasts do not, and the crisis claim has been formally retracted in `ROADMAP.md` — do not reintroduce it from this table. Second, the crisis bucket is the smallest and therefore the least stable: with ~9% of the window it takes only a handful of relabelled turning-point days to move its mean substantially, so a crisis-state ranking should be checked against the alternative regime estimator (`configs/regime_lstm_hmm.yaml`) before it is reported as a finding.

Which architecture leads varies by state (calm: **Regime-LSTM-A-RVonly**; transitional: **Regime-LSTM-B**; crisis: **Regime-LSTM-A**), and the best pooled model overall is **LSTM-RVonly**, which is *not* regime-aware. The mixture-of-experts (Regime-LSTM-B) trains one LSTM per regime, so the crisis expert's *effective* sample is small (crisis ≈ 9% of days), which caps its specialisation — a limitation worth stating rather than hiding, and a reason the feature approach can lead in the crisis rows.

## Gate criteria

- [x] Approach A (regime-as-feature) and Approach B (regime-expert MoE) built, both on the causal filtered posterior; leakage discipline reused from Phase 3 (train-only scaling, windows end before target, gate lagged to t−1).

- [x] Four-way+ comparison vs GARCH/EGARCH/HAR-RV/RW-RV/LSTM/LSTM-RVonly on identical splits; predictions persisted.

- [x] Per-regime (calm/transitional/crisis) error breakdown — core for RQ2.

- [x] Formal Diebold–Mariano (HLN-corrected, Student-t) on the head-to-head pairs, plus a Model Confidence Set (Hansen–Lunde–Nason 2011) over all models for multiple-comparison control (Ch2 §2.7).

- [x] Milestone + figures + reproducible config snapshot.
